feedback: If the learner says all animals have bones inside: a beetle's support is a hard outer case (exoskeleton), and worms and jellyfish have no bones at all.
If the learner is unsure why a jellyfish can't stand: it has no rigid internal skeleton to hold its shape up against gravity.
activities.intendedInsight: A bony internal skeleton is one solution among several for support and protection — some animals have a hard external skeleton and some, like worms and jellyfish, have no bones or hard skeleton at all — so 'having a bony skeleton' is not universal and 'hard bits outside' are not bones inside.
learnerActions: Look side by side at a human (bony skeleton inside), a beetle (hard case outside), and an earthworm or jellyfish (no bones).
Describe where the hard supporting structure is for each: inside the body, outside the body, or with no hard parts at all (soft bodies held in shape by fluid or water).
Answer: why can't a jellyfish stand up the way you can — what does your body have that it doesn't?
Explain why an insect's hard shell is NOT the same as having bones inside.
activities.title: Compare body plans: endoskeleton, exoskeleton, no hard skeleton

feedback: If the learner predicts the top muscle pushes the arm straight: feel the triceps at the back of the upper arm tighten as you straighten against resistance — that muscle pulls the bone while the biceps relaxes.
On the matching task: check that skull→brain and ribcage→heart and lungs are paired correctly.
Watch for the idea that 'muscles push the bone' — use it as a cue to re-feel the arm and re-run the elbow rig.
activities.intendedInsight: When you actively straighten your arm (for example, against resistance) the triceps at the back of the upper arm pulls, not the biceps pushing — muscles pull in opposition, and naming/sorting bones by function consolidates the three jobs.
learnerActions: Bend your arm and feel the biceps on top harden; then straighten it.
PREDICT which muscle tightens to straighten the arm, and say why.
Straighten the arm against a little resistance (e.g. press your hand down on a table or against a partner's hand) and feel the back of your upper arm — notice the triceps tightening.
Explain what has to happen to move the bone back, given that a muscle can only pull.
Sort a set of bones by their job (support / protect / move), and match each protective bone to the organ it guards.
activities.title: Predict–observe–explain: which muscle straightens the arm?
